hook.line: There is a moment before you do something a little scary: sing, call her, say yes. Spanish has one verb for plucking up the nerve, and one for giving someone that push. Vale uses both on Tomás.
hook.en: Go on, come along! (to a friend)

examples.es: Por fin me animé a hablarle.
examples.en: I finally plucked up the courage to talk to her.
Are you up for coming with us? (to a friend)

examples.es: Tomás no se anima a vender el café.
examples.en: Tomás can't bring himself to sell the café.

examples.es: Vale me animó a probar la receta.
examples.en: Vale encouraged me to try the recipe.

rule:
*Animarse a* means to go for it: *me animé a hablarle*, I finally dared to talk to her. After *a*, always use the infinitive.

*Animar a alguien a* is the push from outside: *Vale me animó a probar*, Vale encouraged me to try.

The small word makes the difference: with *me animé*, you did the daring; with *me animó*, someone else cheered you on. It is never "animated" as in English. And *¡Ánimo!* by itself is a cheer.
smallPrint: Teachers call *animarse* a pronominal verb: the *se* version means you motivate yourself.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After *animarse* the verb needs *a* before the infinitive.
*Me animó* says someone else encouraged you; for your own courage, use *me animé*.

personal: Say one thing you finally dared to do. Use *Por fin me animé a*.
